cover.title: API Interview Questions
cover.subtitle: The Backend & SDE Handbook
cover.tagline: 60+ handwritten Q&As on the API questions interviewers ask most. For backend and SDE candidates.
pills: REST, HTTP methods and status codes
Auth with JWT and OAuth 2.0, plus CORS and security
Pagination, rate limiting, caching and gateways
Webhooks, idempotency, versioning, scale and design scenarios

blocks.q: Q1. What is a REST API and what are its core constraints?
a_bullets: ==REST API== exposes resources as URLs, moving representations over HTTP
**Client-server**, **stateless**, cacheable, layered system
Uniform interface: URIs, verbs, representations; optional code on demand

blocks.q: Q2. What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
a_bullets: REST is an ==architectural style==, usually JSON over HTTP; SOAP is a strict XML protocol
SOAP: XML envelope, WSDL contract, built-in WS-Security
REST: lightweight, cacheable, any data format
SOAP suits formal enterprise and banking integrations

blocks.q: Q3. What does it mean that REST is stateless, and why does it matter?
a_bullets: ==Stateless==: every request carries all context, no client session stored between calls
Auth token travels with **every** request
Any server handles any request; scales horizontally; a crash loses no session

blocks.q: Q4. What is the difference between REST and GraphQL?
a_bullets: REST has many fixed endpoints; ==GraphQL== has one endpoint, client asks for exact fields
REST can over-fetch or need several round trips
GraphQL: one query, exact shape, typed schema
REST caches easily via HTTP; GraphQL needs extra work

blocks.q: Q5. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
a_bullets: **PUT** replaces the whole resource; **PATCH** changes only the fields you send.
PUT sends the full representation; a missing field is reset or removed

blocks.q: Q6. What is the difference between GET and POST?
a_bullets: **GET** reads without changing anything; **POST** sends data to create or trigger something.
GET: no body, cacheable. POST: body, not cached
Never put secrets in a GET URL

blocks.q: Q7. Which HTTP methods are safe and which are idempotent?
a_bullets: **Safe** never changes server state; **idempotent** gives the same end state when repeated.
Safe: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD; POST and PATCH not guaranteed

blocks.q: Q8. Why is PUT idempotent but POST not?
a_bullets: PUT targets a **known URL** with full state, so repeats overwrite with the same data; POST creates a new resource each time.
Fix POST retries with an Idempotency-Key

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: PUT replaces, PATCH edits. GET is safe, cacheable. PUT, DELETE idempotent; POST not.

blocks.q: Q9. What is the difference between 401 and 403?
a_bullets: **401** means the server doesn't know who you are; **403** means it knows you but refuses the action.
401: credentials missing, expired or invalid
403: logged in, but role or scope is too low
Re-login can fix 401, never 403

blocks.q: Q10. What is the difference between 400, 404 and 422?
a_bullets: **400** means the request is malformed, **404** means the target doesn't exist, and **422** means it's well-formed but breaks validation rules.
400: broken JSON, wrong types, missing body
404: the route or resource id is unknown
422: syntax is fine, business rules fail

blocks.q: Q11. When do you return 200, 201, 202 and 204?
a_bullets: Use **200** to return data, **201** after creating a resource, **202** when work is queued, and **204** when there is nothing to send back.
201 carries a `Location` header for the new resource
202 returns a status URL the client polls
204 fits DELETE and PUT with no body

blocks.q: Q12. How do you design a consistent error response format?
a_bullets: Return one JSON envelope for **every** error, with a stable machine code, a human message and a request id.
Clients switch on `code`, never on message text
Add field-level details for validation errors
Never leak stack traces or SQL to clients

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: 401 = who are you? 403 = not allowed. 4xx blames the client, 5xx blames the server. Always return one error shape with a stable code.

blocks.q: Q13. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
a_bullets: ==Authentication== proves who you are; ==authorization== decides what you may do.
AuthN first (password, OTP, token), AuthZ next (roles, scopes, ownership)
Failed AuthN gives 401; failed AuthZ gives 403

blocks.q: Q14. What is a JWT and how is its structure laid out?
a_bullets: A ==JWT== is a signed, self-contained token: three Base64URL parts joined by dots.
{red:Header}: alg, typ; {blue:Payload}: claims `sub`, `exp`, `role`
{green:Signature} (HMAC/RSA) proves no tampering

blocks.q: Q15. What is the difference between session-based and token-based authentication?
a_bullets: Sessions keep state on the ==server==; tokens carry it in the ==client's== token.
Session: cookie holds ID, server looks it up; token: server verifies signature
Tokens scale across servers; sessions revoke easily

blocks.q: Q16. How do you handle JWT expiry, refresh tokens and revocation?
a_bullets: Use a ==short-lived== access token (about 15 minutes) plus a long-lived refresh token.
Rotate refresh token on every use
Revoke via denylist of `jti` or token version
example_code: old refresh token is now invalid

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: AuthN = who, AuthZ = what. JWTs are signed, not encrypted. Short access tokens, rotated refresh tokens.

blocks.q: Q17. What is OAuth 2.0 and what problem does it solve?
a_bullets: ==Delegation framework==: an app acts for you without seeing your password.
Gets a **scoped**, short-lived access token; revoke it without changing your password.
Example: "Sign in with Google" lets a calendar app read events only.

blocks.q: Q18. What are the OAuth 2.0 roles and the authorization code flow?
a_bullets: Four roles: ==resource owner== (user), client (app), auth server (issues tokens), resource server (API checking token).
Client swaps a one-time **code** for a token.
Code travels in the browser; token goes over the back channel.

blocks.q: Q19. What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?
a_bullets: OAuth 2.0 = ==authorization== (what app may access); OIDC adds **authentication** (who the user is).
OIDC adds a signed ID token (JWT); request with `openid` scope.
Access token is for APIs; ID token is for the client.

blocks.q: Q20. Why is PKCE needed, and when do you use client credentials?
a_bullets: ==PKCE== stops a stolen code being redeemed; public clients (SPAs, mobile) must use it.
Client sends hashed `code_challenge`, then raw `code_verifier`.
**Client credentials**: server-to-server, a backend job calls an API as itself.
Never ship a client secret in a browser or mobile app.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: OAuth 2.0 = delegated access with tokens. Auth code + PKCE for users, client credentials for services, OIDC for identity.

blocks.q: Q21. What is CORS and why does the browser enforce it?
a_bullets: A browser rule letting a server say which ==origins== may read its responses
Origin = scheme + host + port; blocks evil.com reading your bank's data
Server opts in with headers; CORS is browser-only, **not** auth

blocks.q: Q22. What is a preflight request and when is it sent?
a_bullets: An automatic ==OPTIONS== request asking if the real call is allowed
Sent for PUT, DELETE, PATCH, custom headers or JSON type
Skipped for simple GET and form POST

blocks.q: Q23. How do you protect an API against OWASP API Top 10 risks like BOLA and injection?
a_bullets: ==Object-level authorization== on every request; treat all input as hostile
**BOLA**: check owner on every object ID
Injection: parameterized queries, schema validation; rate limits, TLS, least privilege

blocks.q: Q24. What is the difference between CSRF and XSS, and how do you prevent each?
a_bullets: ==CSRF== tricks a logged-in browser into unwanted requests; ==XSS== injects script running in your site
Bearer tokens in headers avoid CSRF; defend cookies with SameSite

blocks.q: Q25. What is the difference between offset and cursor pagination?
a_bullets: ==Offset== skips N rows by position; ==cursor== resumes after the last row seen.
Offset: any page number, but drifts on inserts or deletes
Cursor stays stable, suits infinite scroll

blocks.q: Q26. Why does offset pagination get slow on large tables?
a_bullets: The database must **read and discard** every skipped row first.
OFFSET 100000 scans 100,000 rows; cost grows with page depth, not size
Keyset seeks via an index in constant time

blocks.q: Q27. How do you design filtering, sorting and field selection for a list endpoint?
a_bullets: Use ==query parameters== on the collection URL; **whitelist** every allowed field.
Filter `status=active&role=admin`; sort `sort=-created_at,name`
Trim payloads with `fields=id,name,email`

blocks.q: Q28. How do you return pagination metadata and links?
a_bullets: Wrap results in an envelope with ==meta== and ==links==, so clients never build URLs.
Include `next_cursor` or `total` and `limit`; `next`/`prev` links, null at ends
Or use a `Link` header with rel values

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Cursor seeks by index; whitelist filters; return links.

blocks.q: Q29. Why do APIs need rate limiting?
a_bullets: Caps requests per client so no caller starves the API.
==Abuse protection== (brute-force, scraping, DDoS), **fairness**
Cost control and ==plan tiers== (free vs paid)

blocks.q: Q30. What is the difference between token bucket and leaky bucket?
a_bullets: Token bucket ==allows bursts==; leaky bucket forces **steady** outflow.
Token: fixed-rate refill, one token per request, else rejected
Leaky: queue drains at constant rate

blocks.q: Q31. What is the difference between fixed window and sliding window rate limiting?
a_bullets: Fixed counts per clock slot; sliding counts the ==last N seconds==.
Fixed window: 1 counter per minute; boundary flaw gives **2x burst**
Sliding log: all timestamps, no boundary burst
Sliding counter: 2 counters, approximate; smooths, costs more memory

blocks.q: Q32. How do you rate limit across multiple servers, and what do you return when the limit is hit?
a_bullets: Use a ==shared store== like Redis, answer **429** with a retry hint.
Atomic `INCR` or Lua script avoids races; or enforce at gateway
Send `Retry-After` plus remaining-quota headers

blocks.q: Q33. What is the difference between client-side, CDN and server-side caching?
a_bullets: They cache at three distances from your database: the ==browser==, the ==CDN edge== and your own ==server tier==.
Client: private to one user, zero network cost
CDN: shared copy near users, serves public GETs
Server: Redis or in-memory, saves database load

blocks.q: Q34. How do Cache-Control, ETag and conditional requests work?
a_bullets: `Cache-Control` sets how long a response is fresh, then the client revalidates using an ==ETag== validator.
`max-age` is freshness; `no-store` blocks caching entirely
Client sends `If-None-Match` with the saved ETag
Unchanged resource returns **304** with no body

blocks.q: Q35. What is the difference between cache-aside and write-through?
a_bullets: In ==cache-aside== the app loads data into the cache on a miss, while ==write-through== updates the cache on every write.
Cache-aside: lazy fill, first read after expiry is slow
Write-through: cache always fresh, writes cost more
Cache-aside is the common default for read-heavy APIs

blocks.q: Q36. How do you invalidate a cache and avoid a cache stampede?
a_bullets: Delete or update the key on every write, and stop a ==stampede== by letting only one request rebuild an expired hot key.
Use TTLs as a safety net for missed invalidations
Add random jitter so keys do not expire together
A short lock lets one rebuild while others wait

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Cache close to the user with `Cache-Control` and ETags, fill server caches with cache-aside, and invalidate on write with TTL jitter to prevent stampedes.

blocks.q: Q37. What is an API gateway and what does it do?
a_bullets: ==API gateway== = single entry point for shared edge concerns
Routes requests; handles auth, rate limits, TLS once
Aggregates, caches and logs responses

blocks.q: Q38. What is the difference between an API gateway and a load balancer?
a_bullets: LB ==spreads traffic== across identical servers; gateway ==understands the API==, policy per route
LB: L4/L7, healthy instance; gateway: path, key, version
Goal: spread load vs API policy; knows hosts, health vs routes, users, keys
Does: balance, failover vs auth, quota, transform
Examples: NGINX, ALB vs Kong, AWS API Gateway; gateways often front several LBs

blocks.q: Q39. What is a webhook and how does it differ from polling?
a_bullets: ==Webhook== = HTTP callback: provider POSTs to your URL on an event
Polling wastes calls, adds delay; webhooks push, near real time, cheaper
Receiver must be public and always up
Flow: {orange:Event} payment paid → {blue:Provider} POST + signature → {green:Endpoint} verify, 200 fast → {purple:Queue} process async

blocks.q: Q40. How do you make webhooks secure and reliable?
a_bullets: Prove each call with a ==signature==, ack fast, make processing repeat-safe
Verify HMAC of raw body with shared secret
Check timestamp to block replay attacks
Dedupe by event id; providers retry on failure

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Gateway = front door with policy; LB = spread load. Webhooks push events: verify signature, reply fast, dedupe by id.

blocks.q: Q41. What is idempotency and why does it matter for payment APIs?
a_bullets: An ==idempotent== operation gives the same result however often repeated
Networks time out, so clients **retry** blindly
Without it, one retry means a double charge
GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not

blocks.q: Q42. How do you implement an Idempotency-Key header?
a_bullets: Client sends a unique key; server runs ==once==, replays saved response
Store key, request hash, response, with a TTL
Same key, different body: return **422**
Lock the key so parallel retries can't both run

blocks.q: Q43. What are the ways to version an API, and which do you prefer?
a_bullets: Version in ==URI path==, header, or query parameter; I prefer path
Path is visible, easy to route, cache-friendly
Header keeps URLs clean but hides the version
Version only on breaking changes, not every release

blocks.q: Q44. What counts as a breaking change, and how do you deprecate an endpoint?
a_bullets: A ==breaking change== fails a working client; give notice, a **Sunset** date, then remove
Announce early; send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers
Track who still calls the old version; keep both live through migration
Idempotency keys make retries safe; versions make change safe
Remove or rename fields only in a new version

blocks.q: Q45. How do you handle large file uploads in an API?
a_bullets: Send ==chunks== straight to object storage; the API never buffers the file
**Multipart**: parallel parts, retry only the failed one
**Resumable**: client asks which parts arrived, continues
Validate size, type, checksum before complete

blocks.q: Q46. What is a presigned URL and why use it?
a_bullets: A ==temporary signed link== to upload or download one object, no credentials needed
Bytes skip your API: servers stay light and cheap
Scope it: one key, one method, **short** expiry
Signature is in the query string, so never log it
example_code: # server signs, client PUTs to S3

blocks.q: Q47. What is the difference between unit, integration and contract testing for APIs?
a_bullets: They differ in ==scope==: one function, real components together, agreed request/response shape
**Unit**: fast, mocked dependencies, many
**Integration**: real DB and HTTP, fewer, slower
**Contract**: consumer and provider can't drift apart

blocks.q: Q48. How do you test an API's auth, error paths and rate limits?
a_bullets: Automate ==negative tests==: send the bad request, assert exact status and error body
**Auth**: no token 401, wrong role 403, expired 401
**Errors**: bad input 422, missing id 404, dependency down 503
**Limits**: exceed quota, expect 429 + `Retry-After`

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Upload **direct to storage** with presigned URLs and chunks. Test unhappy paths: 401, 403, 422, 429.

blocks.q: Q49. What metrics should you monitor for an API (RED and the golden signals)?
a_bullets: ==RED== per endpoint: Rate, Errors, Duration; golden signals add Saturation
Rate per route; errors: 5xx share, 4xx spikes
Duration: p50, p95, p99, never just average; saturation: CPU, memory, pool, queue depth

blocks.q: Q50. What is the difference between logging, metrics and tracing?
a_bullets: Three pillars: ==logs== what happened, ==metrics== how much, ==traces== where
Logs: structured JSON events with request ID
Metrics: cheap numeric series, ideal for alerts; traces: one request's path across services
Flow: metric alert (p99 high) → trace (slow span) → log (error detail)

blocks.q: Q51. What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling for APIs?
a_bullets: Vertical: one server gets more CPU or RAM; ==horizontal== adds servers behind a load balancer
Vertical: simple, but ceiling and downtime
Horizontal: near-unlimited, needs stateless services; state moves to Redis or the database

blocks.q: Q52. How do you find and fix a slow API endpoint?
a_bullets: Measure first: trace the slow span, fix the biggest cost, usually the ==database==
Check p99 and traces; `EXPLAIN` queries, add indexes, kill N+1
Then cache, paginate or move work to a queue

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Alert on RED, debug with traces and logs, scale out stateless services, always measure before optimizing.

blocks.q: Q53. How would you design a URL shortener API?
a_bullets: ==POST /links== creates a code; ==GET /{code}== redirects with 302 or 301.
Generate the code from a **base62** counter, which avoids collisions.
Cache hot codes in Redis (reads far outnumber writes); extras: expiry, custom aliases, click counts.

blocks.q: Q54. How would you design a payment API that never double-charges?
a_bullets: Require an ==Idempotency-Key== on every charge; a retry returns the first result.
Store the key with a **UNIQUE** constraint to block races.
Charge and record in one transaction; reconcile via provider webhooks.

blocks.q: Q55. How would you design a notification or feed API that handles millions of requests?
a_bullets: Keep writes ==async== through a queue; serve reads from precomputed, cached feeds.
Use **cursor** pagination, since offset slows down at scale.
Fan out on write for normal users, on read for celebrities; push via webhooks or WebSockets, not polling.

blocks.q: Q56. How do you make APIs resilient with timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers?
a_bullets: Bound every call with a ==timeout==, retry only transient errors, stop calling a failing dependency.
Back off **exponentially** with jitter to avoid retry storms.
Retry only idempotent or keyed calls; a breaker opens after repeated failures, then probes to recover.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Idempotent writes, cached cursor-paged reads, and every dependency call bounded by timeouts, jittered retries and a breaker.

items: ==Idempotency==: `Idempotency-Key` on POST payments; ==retries== backoff + jitter, idempotent only
==Versioning==: `/v1` path, `Sunset` header; ==Ops==: RED metrics, trace IDs, p99 alerts; HTTPS, object ownership, validate input

blocks.title: TOP 5 MUST-KNOW:
blocks.text: PUT vs PATCH, 401 vs 403, JWT vs session, cursor vs offset, idempotency keys.

caption.text:
The API interview questions they will ask you, answered in handwritten notes.

Backend and SDE interviewers keep coming back to the same topics. This carousel covers them:

• REST and HTTP fundamentals, methods, status codes and error handling
• Authentication, JWT and OAuth 2.0
• CORS and API security
• Pagination, filtering, rate limiting and throttling
• Caching, API gateways and webhooks
• Idempotency and versioning
• File uploads and API testing
• Monitoring and scalability
• Real-world API design scenarios, plus a cheatsheet to revise from

Save this for your next interview prep session and send it to a friend who is preparing too.

Which API question do you find hardest? Tell me in the comments.

Comment “api” to get all the answers as a PDF.
